draft.title: Matter waves
card: De Broglie proposed that particles such as electrons have a wavelength, just as light behaves as both a wave and a particle. The wavelength is λ = h/mv, where h is Planck's constant, m is mass and v is speed.
A larger momentum (mv) gives a shorter wavelength. A moving cricket ball has a wavelength far too small to detect, so only tiny particles such as electrons show wave effects.
Electrons fired at a thin crystal or through slits produce a diffraction pattern. Only waves do this, so the pattern confirmed that matter has wave properties.
Schrödinger built a wave model of the atom. It describes the electron as a wave around the nucleus, not as a particle on a fixed path.
draft.remember: Moving matter has a wavelength λ = h/mv, and electron diffraction showed it is real.

a.q: What did electron diffraction show about electrons?
opts: They can behave as waves
They carry a negative charge
They orbit the nucleus in fixed paths
They have the same mass as a proton
a.why: A diffraction pattern is produced only by waves, so it showed that electrons have wave properties. Negative charge is true, but it was shown by other experiments and is not what a diffraction pattern reveals.
a.clue: Which kind of motion produces a diffraction pattern?

b.q: An electron and a proton move at the same speed. Which statement about their de Broglie wavelengths is correct?
opts: The electron's is longer, because its mass is smaller
The proton's is longer, because its mass is larger
They are equal, because the speeds are equal
Neither has one, because only light has a wavelength
b.why: With λ = h/mv, at equal speed a smaller mass gives a longer wavelength. The electron has much less mass than the proton, so its wavelength is longer. Thinking a heavier particle has a longer wavelength reverses the relationship, because mass is in the denominator.
b.clue: Mass is on the bottom of the fraction in λ = h/mv.

b.best: The electron's is longer, because its mass is smaller

problems.detail: "So only tiny particles such as electrons show wave effects" could suggest that large objects have no wave nature. All moving matter has a wavelength. For large objects it is simply too small to detect. Saying "only tiny particles show detectable wave effects" would be clearer.

check.summary: Both questions are sound, each with one clear answer. One card line could suggest that large objects have no wave nature at all, rather than a wavelength too small to detect.
